chapter: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
title: Marching in St. Agnes band funerals and stopping at the edge of White town
summary: He describes snares muffled on slow dirges, musicians drinking moonshine during the service, and halting at the boundary of the white section; Hinton notes his nickname Pump.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Now, like when St. Agnes's band used to play all these funerals -- we would meet at the hall, at the rehearsal hall where the band used to rehearse at, which was the parish hall of St. Agnes Church. We would meet there, and say, the funeral was going to start at two o'clock -- well, we would meet at 12:30, the band would meet there, and naturally you belonged to a couple of lodges -- at least one lodge. So the band would assemble at the parish hall and march down to the lodge hall, and go to the lodge hall -- all the lodge members would be there, and would line up, and then we would march back to the home to pick up the body.

Now we were liable to play any of Sousa's marches, going to the lodge hall and going to the home, but now, when we leave the home with the body, we take the snares off the drum, which was a field drum, and took the snares off and took a handkerchief and put the handkerchief around the snares so there would be no vibration at all - just a dead sound.
And we would play a tune like "Free as a Bird," you know, dum da da da, da -- we would play that, or we would play "Abide With Me" -- a tune like that, and march slowly to the church.

Now, while the service is going on, see, all of the musicians, and there was a lot back there -- this was during the time of Prohibition, it was still Prohibition, see, and all of the guys in the band would go to one of the moonshine houses where they sold moonshine, and everybody would be sitting up there, because they would leave one guy that didn't drink; they would leave him so he could keep up with the service and let them know what time to get back.
And so he would sit there, and a lot of them would drink so much that by the time the service was over, they could hardly walk!
But anyway, this is what would happen. They would come back, and they would take the body out of the church, and we would march to a slow dirge slowly until we got almost to the White town,
Right where the boundary line was.

Well, the White town at that time was like, 21st Terrace and 6th Avenue. So that's where we were stopped. And they would open up an aisle, like the band would split and half of one side and one on the other side, and the lodge members; all of those that wasn't going to the graveyard, they would all do the same thing.

And the cars would slowly drive through while we would still play this dirge; piece, they would slowly go through until the last car got through there, and that's when the drummer would roll off and would either play "The Saints" or "Onward Christian Soldiers." We never played Ditty Ramble; I don't ever remember playing that.
Well, why did you come through this White town?
Well, that's where the black section of town finished.

And that's where the white section started, so we couldn't go marching through there playing the dirge, those pieces, so we stopped right here and they let the cars go. The graveyard was like about 10 miles out of town, and we had to go through White town to get there.
I see. I just wanted to mention, you
called me Pump, which is my nickname from the Cab Calloway era.
Well, I always forget about the Milton
No, that's okay. I just wanted it on the record, so they knew who that was.
